doc.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

chapter: Rock era, electric piano, move east
title: Electric Wurlitzer and hauling equipment
summary: Roy takes an electric piano because club pianos were bad, then tires of the cables and equipment and returns to acoustic.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well one of the reasons I changed was that some of the clubs we were working had these terrible pianos. Like they have a baby grand, it’s five feet long, and it sounds like it’s strung with rubber bands, and there’s no music in it. You hit a note and it goes duh, instead of ding. So I said well the only thing I can do, I’ll get an electric piano, I’ll carry my own, it’ll be dependable, it’ll be in tune, I’ll have the same instrument to play on. So we did that. We had also a bunch of sound equipment.
That part, that gets a lot of fun, doesn’t it.
It was fun, and we really enjoyed it for a couple of years, but then all of a sudden it got to be a big chore. Because we did not have somebody to come and set the stuff up.
The drummer and I did all the schlepping.
Did you have a Fender Rhodes or a Wurlitzer?
No I had a Wurlitzer that I had re-worked, where you could plug it directly into an amplifier with a volume foot pedal, and a sustain pedal on it. So it was really a wonderful piano.
And that was closest to an acoustic I think at the time.

And the drummer and I would just take all this equipment, we had great big column speakers and we’d put them in cases lined with foam and up on top of this big monster Chrysler station wagon we had, and lash it all down and cover it with canvas, and, next gig, yo!
I mean you know, that’s why he had trouble with his back for a while. But that got to be very difficult. And so finally we just, and then we started working better clubs.
The hardest part was the miles of cable to collect after the gig.
Especially when people spill beer on them.

Yeah, oh please. But we finally gave that up because we started working better clubs too. As we were going along nicer clubs started opening that were bringing in music, so we felt that the pianos got better at the same time, and they weren’t such a problem. So Roy was happy to get that.
Besides, I started to miss the real piano sound.
Nothing like it after you go away from it and you say, after a while, this little thing.
So the other thing was cute and funny for a hot minute. But it was a hot two years, but I mean it was fun. Back to the acoustic and that was great, we enjoyed going back.
